headline: Japanese yen near historical lows; Bank of Japan under pressure to hike in September but significant yield gap versus other major central banks limits any meaningful yen recovery
reasoning: Richardson notes the yen is near historical lows against the USD, with G20 discussions between Bassett and Japanese finance ministers focused on ensuring yen stability and pressuring the Bank of Japan to hike rates in September. However, even with intervention and a potential rate hike, Japan remains significantly behind the global yield curve relative to other major central banks, including the US and Australia. This structural yield gap means any meaningful or sustained yen recovery is unlikely until Japan undertakes longer-term rate hikes. The AUD/JPY carry trade continues to be supported in this environment.
quote: Yeah, there's been commentary coming out of the G20 summit with Bassett and key Japanese finance ministers meeting and talking again and promising to ensure the stability of the Japanese yen. And, um, really, I guess putting some pressure on the Bank of Japan to hike rates in September. That will be a key meeting for overall yen performance. If we do see a rate hike in September, that is going to perhaps alleviate some of the pressure that the yen is facing. But given that we are seeing US yields rise, Australian yields rise. Japan still remains significantly behind the overall yield curve when compared with other major central banks. So even with interventionist policies, you can't see any real significant downturn in the value of the yen at this point.

headline: Fed rate hike back in focus after Kevin Walsh's hawkish Jackson Hole comments; ~70% probability of September hike priced in, with non-farm payrolls as the critical next marker
reasoning: The USD underperformed through August after Treasury Secretary Scott Bassett indicated a government bond buyback program, which dampened Fed rate hike expectations. However, comments from Fed's Kevin Walsh at Jackson Hole were decidedly hawkish, firming expectations back to around 70% probability of a September hike. Walsh pulled back on forward guidance, making upcoming data releases — especially non-farm payrolls — even more important. A soft payrolls print would reduce rate hike expectations and could support AUD above the 72-cent handle.
quote: Yeah we've seen the US dollar underperformed through August after Scott Bassett the Treasury secretary secretary, indicated that the government did plan to begin that government bond buyback program. And that did dampen expectations for fed rate hikes as well. But with Walsh's comments on Friday, those expectations have firmed again, and we are pricing in about a 70% chance at this stage for a rate hike in September. So perhaps that Australian dollar gain that we saw through August now will be more reliant on domestic factors.

headline: AUD yield advantage gathering momentum; RBA rate hike expectations firming as inflation stays stickier than expected, driven by Middle East energy crisis and AI-driven cost pressures

Supply-side inflation is proving stickier than expected due to elevated energy prices from the Middle East conflict and AI-driven energy demand. GDP data on Wednesday and further local inflation data are critical markers for how much further the RBA can hike. The carry trade appeal of the AUD, particularly against the yen, is also supporting the currency.
quote: And we'd expect that yield advantage of the Australian dollar is starting to gather some momentum again. And it has been one of the better performers through the last 3 or 4 weeks, particularly through August, not just against the US dollar but against other key majors as well. And it's that yield support and the expectations of further tightening from the RBA that's lending that markets are really now putting aside the tensions in the Middle East in terms of currency performance at this stage. He sees this as a key shaper of the broader global growth outlook, noting that if softness continues through the back half of the year and into 2027 as a result of the conflict, it would create a difficult macro backdrop for risk currencies like the Australian dollar.
quote: The crisis in the Middle East is putting a cap on those gains and a really extended run beyond sort of $0.70 at the moment. The longer it goes, the bigger pressures we're going to see on energy markets and energy prices. And not just that, but refined, particularly refined costs of diesel. headline: NZD outperformance likely temporary as stagflation and energy crisis cap longer-term upside
reasoning: The New Zealand dollar has outperformed recently on the back of lower US inflation and a more hawkish RBNZ following its last policy meeting. Energy-driven inflation is expected to keep short-term rate pressure elevated, but New Zealand's status as a net energy importer and ongoing stagflation dynamics limit the durability of any rate-driven NZD strength. Richardson argues that any rate hikes will likely need to be unwound relatively quickly once price pressures stabilise, as the RBNZ will then need to shift focus back to stimulating growth.
quote: I'm not sure it changes the longer term outlook for the New Zealand dollar, and it potentially does add a cap to that, given New Zealand is so reliant as a net energy importer, particularly across oil. And the fact that the New Zealand economy continues to suffer the effects of stagflation, any change in those interest rates is likely to be potentially temporary as an impact to try and get down these inflationary pressures led by the energy crisis, and will likely need to be unwound relatively quickly as soon as we do start to see price pressures stabilise in a bid to try and stimulate some growth there in the New Zealand economy.

headline: Sterling faces ongoing pressure as Burnham government's fiscal flexibility spooks bond markets ahead of November budget
reasoning: Matt Richardson notes that the initial appointment of Andy Burnham as UK Prime Minister prompted a sterling sell-off, as his comments about maintaining fiscal policy with 'flexibility' were interpreted by markets as a potential loosening. The appointment of Healey as Chancellor, seen as more market-friendly, steadied the initial sell-off. However, Richardson says markets will closely scrutinise fiscal spending policies ahead of the November budget, particularly given concerns around UK debt levels approaching GDP and prior gilt market volatility under previous fiscal blowouts. The longer-term sterling view hinges on what the Burnham government's actual fiscal policies look like.
quote: Initial movements for the pound were to see a sell off. We did see Andy Burnham in his initial comments outside Downing Street, suggests that he would look to obviously maintain the government's current fiscal policies, but look for flexibility within those. I think that was interpreted by the market as being a loosening, potentially, yes. And that's what did spook markets. And we did see an initial sell off in the pound as bond prices fell and UK gilts rose. But since his appointment of Healey as the Chancellor of the Exchequer, he's expected to be more market friendly than perhaps some of the other candidates that were in line for that position. And that has worked to steady that initial sell off that we've seen. But the market focus really will be on what the Burnham government and what his policies do look like when it comes to fiscal spending, and will be keeping a close eye on commentary leading into the budget in November in shaping that longer term sterling view.
